e.t: “Angith,” also rendered “Anggith,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in four occurrences: three in 1 Kings and one in 1 Chronicles. The available information establishes the name and its locations, but not an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative.

This noun refers to injury or injustice—wrongdoing that harms another person or violates what is right. It describes a condition or act marked by wrong, rather than fairness or righteousness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 199 times, most often in the Old Testament portion of the LXX, and its repeated use shows that the idea applies broadly to human conduct and the condition of societies. The word appears in passages ranging from Genesis to the Psalms and later Greek Old Testament writings.

This Greek LXX noun means “gathering”: an assembling or collected group of people or things. It names the gathering itself rather than describing an action someone performs. In the supplied Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 3:13. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here, but its basic idea remains a gathering or assembled group.

This noun refers to “shouting in harvest,” describing the cries or loud calls associated with gathering crops. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Jeremiah, so its meaning is tied to a harvest setting rather than being a broad term for every kind of speech or sound. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea is a harvest-time shout or cry.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut off the extremities” or “mutilate.” It describes a severe physical act involving the removal or damaging of a person’s bodily extremities. As a verb, it expresses the action itself rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage is determined by the surrounding verse and passage.

“Haleluyah” is an interjection—the familiar exclamation “hallelujah.” It functions as a brief spoken expression rather than as the name of a person, place, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 22 times: 21 times in the Old Testament portion and once in 3 Maccabees. It appears especially often in Psalms, including several psalm openings. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Amitaal is a proper name identifying a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it is rendered “Amitaal” and occurs once, in Jeremiah 52:1. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive term, its ordinary function is to identify someone, not to express an action, quality, or command. The available information does not establish an additional meaning for the name itself, so it is best understood simply as the person’s name in that passage.

This verb means “nurture” or “bring up,” describing the care and raising of someone. It refers to the work of providing upbringing rather than merely naming a person or place. In this Greek corpus, it occurs three times, all in deuterocanonical writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the active care involved in raising and sustaining someone.

This Greek LXX noun means “controversy”: a matter involving opposing positions or contention. It names the issue of disagreement rather than describing a person or action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Ecclesiastes 8:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning remains a controversy or contested matter.

gl: go of one's own accord; desert
d: go of one's own accord; desert

e.t: This verb means to go of one’s own accord or to desert—to leave voluntarily rather than remain with a group or cause. It can describe a person withdrawing or abandoning an association. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Proverbs and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is voluntary departure or desertion.

This verb means “unload”: to take a load, burden, or cargo off or out of something. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 24:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic idea is the removal of what has been carried or transported.

e.h: Unbroken or Not to Be Broken
e.t: This adjective describes something unbroken or not to be broken. It points to a condition of remaining intact, whole, or resistant to being shattered. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:9. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise force in that sentence cannot be described further; its basic meaning remains the quality of being unbroken or impervious to breaking.

The word means “soot,” the dark powdery residue left by smoke or fire. It is a noun naming a visible substance, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Lamentations 4:8. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding context; its basic lexical meaning remains soot.

Asmōth, also rendered Azmoth, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. Its meaning is therefore its identifying name, and the available information does not establish whether it names a person, place, or something else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: three times in 1 Chronicles and once in Ezra. The spelling may appear as Asmoth or Azmoth, but both renderings refer to this same named entity.

This noun refers to security or certainty—the condition of being safe, dependable, and firmly established. It can describe confidence that circumstances will remain secure rather than exposed to danger or instability. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 16 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing that it expresses a recurring concern in biblical language. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains settled security or reliable certainty.

This LXX word is a proper name for “Baiththame,” also given as “Veththame.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action word. The form appears only once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Joshua 19:38, so it identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing a broad concept used throughout Scripture. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific setting.

Beelmaōn is a proper name, referring to a named place or location rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It is also rendered “Veelmaon.” The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 5:8. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its particular significance in that reference cannot be described further; its lexical function is simply to identify the named place associated with the passage.

Berzaith, also known as Verzeth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 7:31. The available information identifies it as a name, but does not provide the surrounding verse text or additional explanation of the person or place it identifies. Its precise reference therefore depends on reading that passage in context.

Bosoran is a proper name, referring to a person or place identified by that name rather than expressing an action, quality, or ordinary object. The form is also given as “Vosoran,” another approved rendering of the same name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 21:27. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a name.

Gaalla is a proper name, referring to a specific named person, place, or other entity rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 12:21. The available lexical information identifies the name itself but does not specify from the name alone whether Gaalla refers to a person, location, or another named subject. Its precise reference is therefore determined by the surrounding verse and passage.

This LXX noun names a small fur-bearing animal: a “weasel” or “marten.” It refers to an animal identified among the creatures mentioned in Leviticus 11:29. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament material represented here, so its ordinary meaning is clear, while its precise role in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage. It is a name for the creature itself, not an action or quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “sweetness”—the pleasant, sugary quality found in something sweet. It names a quality rather than an action, person, or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs twice: once in Judges and once in Wisdom. The word can therefore describe sweetness as a quality recognized in something that brings a pleasant taste or experience. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This proper name refers to Goliath, also rendered “Goliad.” It is a personal name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times: twice in 1 Samuel and twice in Psalms. The name appears in passages connected with the biblical figure known by this name, but the precise force of each occurrence belongs to its surrounding verse and passage. “Goliad” and “Goliath” are variant English renderings of the same name.

Dani, also given as Thani, is a proper name. It identifies a named person or entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Judges 13:2. The available lexical meaning is limited to these name forms, so its precise referent must be identified from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name itself.

This noun means “fear” or “affright”—an experience of being frightened or filled with alarm. It names the emotional response itself rather than an action or command. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:8. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and paragraph, but its basic sense is the presence of fear or sudden alarm.

This Greek LXX verb means to “carry over”—to move or transport something from one place to another. It describes an action of transferring an object or burden rather than merely holding it. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in Joshua, 2 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being moved and where it is taken.

gl: send off in different directions; send to and fro
d: send off in different directions; send to and fro

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “send off in different directions” or “send to and fro.” It describes an action in which someone or something is dispatched away, possibly toward separate destinations or back and forth. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including Proverbs and the books of Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

gl: take good heed to; beware of
d: take good heed to; beware of

e.t: This verb means “take good heed to” or “beware of.” It describes deliberate caution—paying close attention so that a person avoids danger, harm, or a serious mistake. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scripture represented here, it appears three times: twice in Old Testament books and once in 2 Maccabees. Because the available entries do not include verse text, the exact object of the warning must be understood from each surrounding passage. It is a verb expressing active watchfulness, not merely general awareness.

This Greek LXX verb refers to something made into or associated with a “net” or “lattice.” Its basic sense concerns a mesh-like structure formed from connected strands or openings. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at 1 Kings 7:6. Because no verse text is provided, the precise way the word functions in that passage cannot be described further, but its central idea remains a net-like or lattice-like form.

This word means “roe,” an animal term used as a noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:58. The available lexical meaning identifies the word clearly, while the reference locates its single occurrence in the biblical text. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s broader contextual role in that verse cannot be described without adding information beyond its established meaning.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Dōr” or “Thor,” and functions as the name Dor. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs five times in the LXX corpus, appearing in Joshua, Judges, and 1 Chronicles. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is to identify the named place or entity called Dor.

Ezekri is a personal name in the Greek Septuagint (LXX), referring to a particular individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Chronicles 28:7. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly its identification of that person; the name itself does not provide a broader description without the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “send in” or “bring in.” It describes moving someone or something into a place, emphasizing the action of causing entry. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 13:20. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains the act of sending or bringing inward rather than merely sending generally.

This verb means “blind”: to deprive someone of sight or leave a person unable to see. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across seven verses, including passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah. The normal sense remains the direct act of making blind or causing blindness.

gl: commander of a squadron of elephants
d: commander of a squadron of elephants

e.t: This Greek noun means “commander of a squadron of elephants.” It describes a person responsible for directing an organized group of war elephants, rather than referring to the animals themselves. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its precise role in any one passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning identifies an officer overseeing elephant forces.

This noun means an “unguent-box,” a container used to hold ointment or scented oil. It names an object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Job 41:23. The available information establishes its basic meaning and rarity, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the word’s particular function in that passage cannot be described further. Its central idea remains a box or container associated with unguent, meaning a prepared ointment or fragrant oil.

This verb means “send out” or “let.” It describes sending someone or something away, or allowing something to proceed. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs three times, all in 3 Maccabees. The basic sense remains action-oriented: something is released, dispatched, or permitted rather than held back. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “welcome”—to receive someone with acceptance rather than rejection. It describes an act of receiving a person or group favorably. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs 20 times, all in deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on who is being received and the surrounding words, but the central idea remains an open, accepting reception.

This Greek LXX noun means “support”—something that steadies, upholds, or provides a firm basis. It refers to help or reinforcement rather than describing an action by itself. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 2 Samuel 22:19; its precise force there is understood from the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains something that gives strength or stability when support is needed.

This word means “manifest,” referring to something made evident or openly displayed; it can also appear as “Epiphanes.” It functions as either a noun or an adjective, so it may identify a name or describe something that is plainly revealed. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs four times, with each occurrence in a different verse. Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective means “celestial” or “heavenly,” describing something belonging to or associated with heaven rather than the ordinary earthly realm. It identifies the character or setting of what it modifies, so its exact force depends on the noun and surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in Psalms and three times in the Maccabean books. The English rendering “heavenly” appears for one occurrence, supporting the same central meaning.

This verb means “prepare”: it describes making something ready for a person, purpose, or coming event. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for deliberate action rather than a mere intention. The word appears 154 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it has a broad and ordinary range of use. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what is being prepared and the surrounding sentence.

Ephod is the name of a specific biblical object or item, expressed in English by the same word. It functions as a noun rather than an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Judges 8:27. The word itself identifies the ephod, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is happening with it there. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Old Testament translation context.

Zabdiel, also rendered Zavthil, is a personal name. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the name occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles and once in 1 Maccabees. Because the available wording gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, the specific identity and role of each person must be understood from its passage.

This word is a proper name referring to Zeb, also rendered Ziv. It identifies a person rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across three verses, chiefly in Judges and once in Psalms. Because it is a personal name, its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself. The name appears in Judges 7:25, Judges 8:3, and Psalms 82:12.

Thabasōn is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), referring to a person named in 2 Samuel 24:6. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or action word, it does not describe a quality, object, or command. Its significance comes from identifying that individual in the passage. This Greek LXX form occurs once in the available Old Testament corpus.

This Greek Old Testament adjective refers to a dead body or carcass. It describes the remains of a creature after life has ended, especially in passages concerned with contact with dead animals and ritual uncleanness. The word occurs 32 times in the Greek Old Testament, with many occurrences in Leviticus and others in books such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a lifeless body or animal carcass.

This word is a personal name, given as “Idouias; Ithoias.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament data, it appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 4:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is the personal designation itself.

This word means “18” and identifies the Hebrew letter “tsadhe” in the arrangement of Psalm 118. It functions as an indeclinable number rather than as a word describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 118:137. Its role is therefore structural: it marks the eighteenth position in the psalm’s ordered sequence, while the surrounding verse supplies the content associated with that section.

Iōree, also written Ioree, is a proper name—a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 5:13. The available wording identifies the name itself, but does not provide its meaning or explain the person’s role. Therefore, the clearest understanding is simply that Iōree is the personal name preserved in that genealogical or historical record.

This Greek LXX verb means “bad-mouth”: to speak against someone in a harmful or insulting way. It describes wrongful speech directed at another person rather than a neutral statement or simple disagreement. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, appearing in Exodus, 1 Samuel, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains speech that damages another person’s reputation or standing.

This Greek LXX verb means “intoxicated; sleep,” describing becoming drunk or entering sleep. Its basic sense concerns a changed state of awareness or alertness, rather than an action performed on someone else. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Jeremiah 28:39, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples in this corpus. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “going down into” or “descent,” describing movement from a higher place or position downward. It presents the act or process of descending rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 15:13. Because the word appears only once and no verse text is provided here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context. Its central idea remains a downward movement or entry.【p03:word:lxx:L707249:identity】【p03:word:lxx:L707249:occurrences】【p01:word:lxx:L707249:reference:0】

This Greek LXX verb means “mock at”: to ridicule or treat someone with scorn rather than respect. It describes an active response toward a person or message, not merely private disagreement. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in passages from 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains consistent across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines exactly whom or what is being mocked. As a verb, it describes the act of expressing contempt through derision.

This Greek LXX verb means “rise up against,” describing the act of opposing or standing against someone. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 16:3. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself plainly conveys active resistance or opposition. This Greek LXX noun means “settlement,” referring to an established place where people live. As a noun, it names the inhabited place itself rather than an action or person. It occurs 29 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, showing a recurring word for a settled dwelling or community. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kedamoth, also rendered Kethamoth, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 2:26. Because the available information identifies the word as a name rather than a common noun or action, it is best understood as referring to a specific location, not as describing a quality, activity, or spiritual concept. The exact role of Kedamoth in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage and its broader account of Israel’s journey.

This word means “bar,” referring to a solid piece used to close, secure, or reinforce an opening. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including several references in Nehemiah to bars associated with gates and other occurrences in Job and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “bake”: to cook food by heating it, especially prepared food such as bread or cakes. It describes the action of making food ready through baking rather than naming the food itself. This Greek LXX word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both in 2 Samuel 13. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning is the act of baking. [p03:word:lxx:L707793:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L707793:occurrences]

This verb means to hurl someone or something down, emphasizing forceful movement from a higher place to a lower one. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 6:10. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its central meaning remains the forceful act of throwing or casting down.

This adverb describes something flowing or bursting out like a spring—“like a spring; gushing.” It portrays movement or speech as a forceful, abundant outpouring rather than a slow or measured release. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Maccabees 14:45. Because the verse text is not included here, the surrounding context would be needed to identify exactly what is described as gushing in that passage.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Manaim” or “Manem.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament, though the available wording alone does not establish which. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all in 2 Samuel: 17:24, 17:27, and 19:33. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage rather than by the name itself.

Maspharath is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament wording of Nehemiah 7:7. It is preserved as “Maspharath,” with the alternate rendering “Masfarath” also recorded for the same name. The available information identifies it only as a name and does not describe the person or place named, so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding verse. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nehemiah 7:7.

This Greek LXX noun means a “post” or “outpost”—a position established for watching, guarding, or maintaining a presence. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all within 1 Samuel 14, so its use is concentrated in one narrative setting rather than spread broadly across the corpus. The word refers to a stationed place or position, not to a written message sent through the mail. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX conjunction means “neither” or “nor.” It links two or more negative statements, people, things, or possibilities, showing that none of them applies or is included. The word may stand between related clauses or joined items, much like “neither … nor” in ordinary English. It occurs 16 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its exact force in any verse depends on the statements it joins.

Minaios, also rendered Mineos, is a proper name—a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, in five verses, including passages in Chronicles and Job. The name itself does not provide a wider definition beyond identifying the person named; the surrounding verse is needed to understand that individual’s role in each passage.

This word means “belt,” a noun for a band or piece of clothing worn around the body. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears in descriptions of priestly and other garments, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, and Isaiah. Its meaning remains focused on the garment itself rather than an action or quality. It occurs 11 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, including one occurrence in Baruch. [References: Exodus 28:37; Exodus 29:6; Leviticus 8:9; Isaiah 61:10.]

Mosollamia is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal designation. The name occurs three times in the Greek text of 1 Chronicles, specifically in 1 Chronicles 26:1, 26:2, and 26:9. Its exact significance beyond identifying the person is not established by the available lexical information.

This word means “dead,” describing someone or something that is no longer living. As an adjective, it identifies what is dead; as a noun, it can refer to the dead. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 76 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing regular use for this basic condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

The word means “obol,” the name of a monetary unit. It is a noun used when an amount is counted or valued. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, from Exodus through Ezekiel, showing that it belongs to language about measured amounts and payment rather than describing a person, action, or quality. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the monetary term “obol.”

gl: disease whereby the body is drawn back and stiffens; tetanus
d: disease whereby the body is drawn back and stiffens; tetanus

e.t: This word describes a disease in which the body is drawn backward and becomes stiff—a condition identified as tetanus. It is an adjective, so it describes the bodily condition rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 32:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning is the severe physical condition itself.

This conjunction means “that way” or “how,” connecting words or clauses to show the manner in which something happens or is to be understood. It can introduce an expression of method, direction, or manner rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 225 times, so its precise force is shaped by the sentence around it. Its documented usage extends from Genesis through the Epistle of Jeremiah, showing that it is a regularly used connecting word in the LXX.

This Greek LXX noun means “frost,” the thin layer of ice formed when cold air freezes moisture. It names a natural condition rather than an action or emotion. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, appearing in Genesis, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Baruch. Its ordinary meaning remains stable across these occurrences: severe cold expressed through the presence of frost. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what the frost signifies or contributes in any particular passage.

gl: dry and hard all round; exceeding hard
d: dry and hard all round; exceeding hard

e.t: This LXX adjective describes something that is “dry and hard all round” or “exceeding hard.” It presents a quality of strong, thorough hardness rather than softness or moisture. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scripture, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Ezekiel, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains complete, intense hardness or dryness.

This Greek LXX verb means “carry around.” It describes taking or bearing something from place to place rather than leaving it in one location. As a verb, it expresses an action involving movement while carrying. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, across Joshua, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being carried and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of carrying around.

This Greek LXX verb means “squeeze.” It describes the act of applying pressure to something, and it functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Micah and once in Sirach. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context, which is not included here.

This Greek LXX verb means “to travel” or “to go,” describing movement from one place to another. It is used for people who leave, proceed, or journey toward a destination. The word appears 1,089 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, so it commonly expresses ordinary physical movement. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on who is going and where the surrounding passage says they are headed.

This noun means “gateway; entrance,” referring to a passage or access point into a place. It names the entry structure itself rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Amos and once in Zephaniah, showing a specific architectural term used in two prophetic passages. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a gateway or entrance. [Amos 9:1; Zephaniah 1:9]

This Greek LXX adjective means “fire-bearing,” describing something that carries, bears, or is associated with fire. It is a descriptive word rather than the name of an object by itself, so the noun it modifies supplies the specific thing being described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 41:21. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains something that bears or conveys fire.

This word means “whistling,” describing a sharp, rushing, or hissing sound. It functions as a noun or adjective, so it can name such a sound or describe something marked by it.
